title: Distributed frontier and next-best-view exploration
description: Distributed UAV teams combine frontier regions and next-best-view planning to map unknown environments.
introduction: A team can map an unknown environment in parallel, provided its robots choose complementary places to look. This framework combines frontier-based exploration with next-best-view planning, giving each UAV a local planning loop that uses shared team information when communication is available.

problem.heading: More robots need complementary viewpoints.
paragraphs: Sending several UAVs into the same environment can create repeated observations and unnecessary travel. The team needs a way to spread its effort across unexplored regions while each vehicle continues to maintain and update its own map.

The value of an additional UAV also depends on the environment. A compact space may offer fewer opportunities for parallel exploration than a larger, more open area, so team size and deployment conditions matter.

approach.heading: Local planning, informed by the team.
paragraphs: Each UAV uses 3D LiDAR measurements to construct a local OctoMap and detect frontiers at the boundary between known free space and unknown space. Mean-shift clustering groups those frontiers into candidate exploration regions.

When communication is available, robots exchange maps and positions. Distance-based assignment encourages different UAVs to work on different regions. Each robot then selects its next viewpoint using expected information gain, travel cost and the positions of nearby teammates.
The vehicle moves towards the selected viewpoint, updates its map and repeats the process. Planning remains local to each UAV, while exchanged information helps reduce redundant exploration.

evidence.label: Simulation study
evidence.text: The published evaluation compares exploration time and path length in Test City and forest environments using different team sizes. These results come from simulation.

evidence.label: Environment-dependent team size
evidence.text: In the compact Test City scenario, the third UAV brings little additional benefit after the second. The forest scenario offers more scope for parallel exploration. The illustrated trials start the UAVs at the same location, so the conclusion is tied to those deployment conditions.
